("title") or item.get("description") or item.get("label") or item.get("field") or item.get
("field_key") or item.get("contract_number") or "item"`. `daily_digest.py`'s `listing_change_signals()`
items (built by `engine/discovery/tender_changes.py`'s `_event()`, migration 0051) carry BOTH `"title"`
(the tender's own title - r.get("title"), already shown in every other section of the same email -
new_tenders, submission_due) AND `"summary"` - the actual, specific change: `"Closing date extended:
2026-10-20 -> 2026-11-05"`, `"Cancelled by the buyer (...)"`, `"Briefing session moved: ..."`, etc.
Since `"title"` is checked first and is always present, `"summary"` was never reached. Confirmed by
constructing a cancelled-tender item and a closing-date-moved item side by side and rendering both
through the real `render_text()`: both produced the exact same generic line (the tender's own title),
with zero way for the reader to tell a cancellation from a date move from a new addendum without
opening the app - the entire value of this section (see its own docstring: "Cancellations and moved
dates first") defeated in the one place a person actually reads it, their inbox.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, severe).** Every `listing_changes` item in every sent digest email, since this
section was added (migration 0051), rendered with the specific change silently dropped - not a rare
edge case, the UNCONDITIONAL behavior for 100% of real items, since `"title"` is always present on a
real tender record and wins the chain every time.

**Fix:** added one targeted check after the existing `bit` chain: `if item.get("change_type") and
item.get("summary"): bit = f"{bit}: {item['summary']}"`. Keyed off `"change_type"` specifically
because it is confirmed (by grep) unique to `listing_changes` items - `tender_updates` items also
happen to carry an unrelated `"summary"` key (`doc.get("summary")`, the watched document's own
summary, a different meaning entirely) but never `"change_type"`, so they are correctly left
untouched; verified this directly with a negative-control case.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_render_text_shows_what_actually_changed_on_a_listing_change()`
to `engine/notify/test_send_digest_emails.py`: a cancelled-tender item and a closing-date-moved item
both now render with their real, distinguishable change text, plus the `tender_updates`-with-its-own-
`"summary"`-key negative control confirming no cross-section effect. Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting
reproduced the exact predicted 2 failures with every other check (including all of this file's
pre-existing `send_one()`/`main()` checks) still green; restored, `0 failure(s)`. Regression-checked
`engine/notify/test_digest_live.py` and `test_digest_opt_in.py` (real consumers/producers of this
digest shape) - all pass.

**Regression:** `engine/notify/send_digest_emails.py` (one `if` check added inside `render_text()`'s
existing per-item loop, ~13 lines including comment - every item with no `"change_type"` key, i.e.
every section except `listing_changes`, is byte-for-byte unaffected), `engine/notify/
test_send_digest_emails.py` (1 new test function, 3 checks, wired into `main()`). No schema or other
call-site changes - `daily_digest.py`'s own JSON report is unchanged, only how the already-correct
`"summary"` field gets rendered into the plain-text email body.

### Finding 114 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a worker killed in the one-call gap between writing an onboarding document's classification result and marking its upload row 'classified' left that document permanently showing as BOTH "to review" and "couldn't be read - upload again" on the same page, with no way for either the system or the user to clear it)

**Where:** this cycle's "worker/job-queue" rotation, after `poll_loop.py`/`run_bridges.py`'s own
orchestration logic (already thoroughly reviewed the prior two cycles, re-checked again this cycle
from several different angles - stale-job recovery, the `SetupError`-aborts-the-batch design,
registered-bridge completeness, CI wiring, worker image dependency completeness, Scout alert
re-notification correctness - with nothing new found in any of them). `engine/onboarding/
process_onboarding_jobs.py`'s `fail_stale_uploads()`.

**What was tested:** `process_upload()` does its real work in two separate REST calls with no shared
transaction: first `POST onboarding_document_results` (the classification proposal, `review_status:
"pending_review"`), then `PATCH onboarding_uploads` to `status: "classified"`. A worker killed in the
gap between those two calls - a crash, an OOM kill, an ungraceful redeploy, exactly the scenario
`fail_stale_uploads()` exists to recover from - leaves the upload row stuck at `status: "classifying"`
with its result already written. Confirmed directly: constructed exactly this state (a stale
`classifying` row with a matching `onboarding_document_results` row already present) and ran the real
`fail_stale_uploads()` against it - it marked the row `classification_failed` with `"Upload this file
again"`, unconditionally, with no check for whether the work had actually already succeeded.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Traced the real consequence on `app/app/company/document-scan/page.tsx`:
the "To review" list queries `onboarding_document_results` by `review_status = "pending_review"`
alone (no join back to the parent upload's own status), and the "couldn't be read" list queries
`onboarding_uploads` by `status = "classification_failed"` independently - the SAME document would
appear in both simultaneously. Reviewing/applying a result (`actions.ts`'s `markApplied()`) only ever
updates the result row's own `review_status`; it never touches the parent upload row at all - so even
after the user reviews and applies the perfectly good result, the SAME document stays listed as
"failed, upload it again" forever, with no code path that ever clears it. Same bug CLASS (a narrow,
two-separate-writes race leaving one system of record out of sync with another, with no owner or
trace) as Finding 98's `save_readiness_seen_db()` fix, here on the onboarding-scan queue specifically.

**Fix:** `fail_stale_uploads()` now checks, before declaring a stale row failed, whether an
`onboarding_document_results` row already exists for it. If one does, the upload is self-healed to
`status: "classified"` (clearing `classification_error`) instead of wrongly marked failed, with a
`"warning"`-severity alert (a recovery, not a loss) rather than the usual `"error"`. A genuinely dead
row with no result is still marked `classification_failed` exactly as before - verified with a
negative control in the same test.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_fail_stale_uploads_self_heals_a_row_whose_result_was_already_
written()` to `engine/onboarding/test_process_onboarding_jobs.py` (4 checks: the raced row self-heals
to classified with no misleading error, the negative-control dead row still fails, and the alert is a
warning not an error). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted 3 failures
with every other check in the file - including the pre-existing stale-row test's own real-failure
case and every `process_upload()` path test - still green; restored, `0 failure(s)`. Regression-
checked `engine/onboarding/test_classify_documents.py` and `engine/worker/test_poll_loop.py` - all
pass; `py_compile` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/onboarding/process_onboarding_jobs.py` (`fail_stale_uploads()`: one extra GET
plus a conditional branch before the existing fail-path, ~25 lines including comment - a stale row
with NO existing result is byte-for-byte unaffected, matching the pre-existing test case exactly),
`engine/onboarding/test_process_onboarding_jobs.py` (1 new test function, 4 checks, wired into
`main()`). No schema or other call-site changes. The identical two-write race shape exists in
`engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py`'s own `fail_stale_uploads()`/`cv_extraction_results` pair (same
pattern, confirmed by reading it) - left unfixed this pass to keep this fix contained and verified;
flagged in `System-Status.md` as the same bug class, worth a follow-up pass rather than a second,
unverified change bundled into this one.

### Finding 115 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - the RRM-family SANRAL filler computed three real discrepancy/gap WARNINGs correctly but only ever printed them to the worker container's own stdout, so none of the three ever reached the pack's own manifest, the one place a reviewer actually looks)

**Where:** this cycle's SANRAL pack rotation, after `fill_docx_forms.py`/`sanral_b7.py`/`fill_
authority_letter.py`/`company_documents.py` (clean-swept the prior cycle) and `fill_financial_hours.py`
(re-read, already correctly hardened against NaN/Infinity). `engine/fill_tender.py`'s `main()` - the
RRM Consultant Tender family filler (`assemble_pack.py`'s `FILLERS["RRM Consultant Tender"]`).

**What was tested:** `main()` runs three real, computed checks after filling the workbook: (1) Form
B7's own closing date (`TEND 1X!F125`) against the SETUP sheet's own closing date (`SETUP!C3`) - a
genuine discrepancy would mean the template itself disagrees with itself, the same class of signal
`classify_tender.discrepancies()` already surfaces for client-typed-vs-SETUP mismatches elsewhere in
this codebase; (2) each bundled "TENDDER n" row's own YES/NO answer, flagging any that isn't YES; (3)
for a YES row, whether its own Form C2.4 sheet has real tendered figures yet. All three were computed
correctly but only ever `print()`ed - never appended to `notes`, the one list `main()` returns that
`assemble_pack.py` actually folds into the pack's real `warnings`/manifest (confirmed by reading the
call site: `warnings += FILLERS[family].main(...) or []`, then `"warnings": warnings` in the saved
manifest). A background worker's stdout is not a notification channel - the exact "a real check exists
in code but never reaches a real surface" shape this session has found and fixed repeatedly elsewhere
(Finding 91's disabled trigger, Finding 113's dropped `summary` field), here inside a filler that had
never had this specific angle checked before.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** For the RRM family specifically (the minority family by sample count in this
repo, but a real, live SANRAL route `assemble_pack.py` dispatches to), a genuine Form-B7-vs-SETUP
closing-date conflict, a bundled contract whose own template answer isn't YES, or a bundled contract
still missing its real Form C2.4 figures would ALL be silently invisible to anyone reviewing the pack
in the app - visible only in container logs nobody routinely reads. `fill_conventional.py` (the
majority Conventional family) has no equivalent closing-date check at all, confirming this gap was
specific to the RRM filler's own, more thorough diagnostic, not a codebase-wide pattern needing a
wider fix.

**Fix:** factored the three checks into a new, pure `tender_check_notes(close, b7, bundles)` function
(no `Workbook` needed - takes already-read values) returning the note strings; `main()` now appends
its output to `notes` (kept the existing `print()`s too, for log visibility) instead of only printing.
Scoped to `fill_tender.py` only - `fill_conventional.py` was deliberately left alone: adding a brand
new closing-date check there would be a feature addition needing its own real-template verification,
not a "contained issue" fix of something already computed but unsurfaced.

**Verified red-then-green.** New file `engine/test_fill_tender.py` (6 test functions, 8 checks) drives
`tender_check_notes()` directly - no RRM-family sample workbook is committed to this repo (the exact
same limitation `test_fill_b7_legacy_precedence.py`'s own docstring already names for this file's
earlier Finding-81 fix), which is precisely why the checks were factored into a pure function: testable
without one. Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting made the test file's own import crash with
`AttributeError: module 'fill_tender' has no attribute 'tender_check_notes'` (the function didn't exist
yet) - confirmed the test genuinely exercises the new code, not a tautology; restored, `0 failure(s)`.
Regression-checked `engine/test_fill_b7_legacy_precedence.py` (the real, template-backed consumer of
this same module's Form B7 logic) - still `0 failure(s)`, unaffected. `py_compile` clean. Wired the new
test into `bridge-worker-ci.yml` right after the existing Finding-81 B7 step (validated with
`yaml.safe_load` before committing).

**Regression:** `engine/fill_tender.py` (`tender_check_notes()`: new ~25-line pure function; `main()`:
the three checks' control flow is otherwise unchanged, their `print()` output is byte-for-byte
identical - only the previously-missing `extra_notes`/`notes` append is new), `engine/test_fill_
tender.py` (new file, 6 test functions, 8 checks), `.github/workflows/bridge-worker-ci.yml` (1 new
step). No schema or other call-site changes - `assemble_pack.py`'s own handling of `FILLERS[family].
main()`'s return value is unchanged; it simply now receives a fuller list.

### Finding 116 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - the identical race-stuck-queue-row bug Finding 114 fixed in the onboarding scan queue, ported to the CV-extraction queue it was explicitly flagged for)

**Where:** this cycle's CV rotation - a direct, planned follow-up on Finding 114's own documented TODO
("the identical two-write race shape exists in `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py`'s own
`fail_stale_uploads()`/`cv_extraction_results` pair... left unfixed this pass... worth a follow-up
pass rather than a second, unverified change bundled into this one" - `docs/specs/System-Status.md`,
2026-11-01). `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py`'s `fail_stale_uploads()`.

**What was tested:** confirmed the code shape is byte-for-byte the same pattern as `process_
onboarding_jobs.py` before its own fix: `process_upload()` does its real work in two separate,
non-transactional REST calls - POST `cv_extraction_results` (the proposed fields, `review_status:
"pending_review"`), THEN PATCH `cv_uploads` to `status: "extracted"`. Reproduced directly (the exact
same repro Finding 114 used, adapted to this table pair): a stale `extracting` row with a matching
`cv_extraction_results` row already present got marked `extraction_failed` ("upload the CV again"),
unconditionally, with no check for whether the work had actually already succeeded.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Traced the real UI consequence this time too, not assumed from the onboarding
precedent: `app/app/people/[id]/page.tsx` queries `cv_extraction_results` by `review_status =
"pending_review"` and `cv_uploads.status = "extraction_failed"` independently (same pattern as the
onboarding page); `applyCvExtraction` (`app/app/people/actions.ts`) only ever updates `people` and
the result row's own `review_status` - it never touches the parent upload row at all. Same consequence
as Finding 114: a raced CV upload would show as both "pending review" and "extraction_failed - upload
again" at once, permanently, with no code path that ever clears it even after the result is reviewed
and applied.

**Fix:** identical to Finding 114 - `fail_stale_uploads()` now checks for an existing `cv_extraction_
results` row before declaring a stale upload failed; if one exists, self-heals to `status: "extracted"`
(clearing `extraction_error`) with a `"warning"`-severity alert instead of `"error"`. A genuinely dead
row with no result is still marked `extraction_failed` exactly as before.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_fail_stale_uploads_self_heals_a_row_whose_result_was_already_
written()` to `engine/cv/test_extract_cv_fields.py` (4 checks, same shape as Finding 114's own test -
the raced row self-heals with no misleading error, the negative-control dead row still fails, the
alert is a warning not an error). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted 3
failures with every other check in the file - including `test_queue()`'s own real-failure case and
every other `process_upload()`/`poll_once()` path test - still green; restored, `ALL PASSED`.
Regression-checked `engine/cv/test_process_cv_jobs.py` - `0 failure(s)`; `py_compile` clean on both
touched files.

**Regression:** `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py` (`fail_stale_uploads()`: one extra GET plus a
conditional branch before the existing fail-path, ~25 lines including comment - a stale row with NO
existing result is byte-for-byte unaffected), `engine/cv/test_extract_cv_fields.py` (1 new test
function, 4 checks, wired into `main()`; added the module's missing `import datetime`, needed by the
new test only - `fail_stale_uploads()` itself already had its own). No schema or other call-site
changes. Finding 114's own backlog item is now closed - no further follow-up outstanding for this
bug class across the six job queues (all six already had their stale-job-recovery guard fixed
repo-wide for the separate malformed-timestamp bug, Finding 99; this self-heal refinement was
specific to the two queues - onboarding and CV - whose own result table is a SEPARATE row from the
upload row they claim, the shape that makes this exact race possible).

### Finding 117 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a non-string closing_date on any one scored release crashed with a raw TypeError, silently dropping that one roster entry's whole daily digest for the day with no hint which field caused it)

**Where:** this cycle's "notify" rotation. `engine/notify/daily_digest.py`'s `submission_due_signals()`
- zero dedicated test coverage existed for this function before this pass (confirmed by grep - no
`test_daily_digest*.py` file, and neither `test_digest_live.py` nor `test_digest_opt_in.py` exercised
it).

**What was tested:** `submission_due_signals()` reads `r.get("closing_date")` from a scored OCDS
release and calls `closing[:10]` then `datetime.date.fromisoformat(...)`, inside a `try/except
ValueError` that does NOT also catch `TypeError` - the exact same malformed-TYPE (not just malformed-
string) risk `watch_deadlines.days_until()` already has an explicit, documented guard against
elsewhere in this same codebase ("a value that isn't a string at all - a number, bool, or a list/dict
... slips past a bare ValueError catch entirely"). Reproduced directly: a release dict with
`closing_date: 20261115` (an int, not a string) raised `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`
straight out of the function.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Traced the blast radius precisely rather than assuming the worst: `company_
signals()` (which calls this function) runs inside `main()`'s own per-roster-entry `try/except`
(Enterprise-readiness audit round 2, 2026-10-20 - "one bad roster entry... must not cost everyone else
their digest"), so this does NOT take down the whole run - but it DOES silently drop that ONE person's
entire digest for the day (every section, not just "closing soon"), logged only as a generic "could
not build a digest for X: TypeError" alert with no hint it was specifically `closing_date`'s type. No
live incident confirmed (every real scraper's own `closing_date` field traced back to either a plain
`.strip()`'d string or a direct OCDS JSON passthrough, both normally strings or `None`) - fixed
proactively anyway, same reasoning this file's own sibling pass used today for `classify_tender.py`'s
AM/PM closing-time fix: the guard is the exact same cheap, already-proven pattern (`isinstance`-check
+ `system_alerts.record`) this codebase already uses for the identical risk elsewhere, so there is no
real cost to closing the gap before a live incident forces it.

**Fix:** added an `isinstance(closing, str)` check before the existing try/except, mirroring `days_
until()`'s own style - skips the item with a `"warning"`-severity alert naming the real value and
field, instead of letting `TypeError` propagate. The existing `ValueError` path (a malformed-but-
string date, e.g. `"not-a-real-date"`) is completely unchanged.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_submission_due_signals_survives_a_non_string_closing_date()`
to `engine/notify/test_digest_live.py` (4 checks: non-string closing_date skipped + alerted, a real
string closing_date completely unaffected, a malformed-but-string date still handled by the pre-
existing path). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted crash (`TypeError:
'int' object is not subscriptable`, uncaught, aborting the test file's own `__main__` block) -
confirmed the test genuinely exercises the new code, not a tautology; restored, `0 failure(s)`.
Regression-checked `engine/notify/test_digest_opt_in.py`, `test_send_digest_emails.py` - all pass.
`py_compile` clean on both touched files.

**Regression:** `engine/notify/daily_digest.py` (`submission_due_signals()`: one `isinstance` check
added before the existing try/except, ~15 lines including comment - every release whose `closing_date`
is already a string, real or malformed, is byte-for-byte unaffected), `engine/notify/test_digest_
live.py` (1 new test function, 4 checks, wired into the file's own `__main__` block). No schema or
other call-site changes.

### Finding 118 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, severe - fingerprint.py's own advertised "whole-file hash" check was computed, stored, and then never once read: a real content-only template change - a label's wording, a dropdown option's own text - was completely invisible, with the tool reporting "OK: matches" and zero trace)

**Where:** this cycle's SANRAL pack rotation. `engine/fingerprint.py`'s `diff()` - the template-
change check Sarel's own standing rule ("there's always a chance a tender template has changed, so we
must always check first") exists to enforce - plus its two real callers, `engine/intake/classify_
tender.py`'s `check_fingerprint()` (intake time) and `engine/pack/assemble_pack.py`'s `check_template()`
(pack-build time, `build_submission_pack()`'s own STEP 1).

**What was tested:** `build_fingerprint()`'s own return dict includes `file_sha256` (the module's own
docstring lists "whole-file hash" among what it computes and compares), but `diff()`'s actual
comparison list - `family`, `sheet_names`, `zip_part_count`, `dropdown_counts`, `dropdown_total`,
`named_ranges`, `cell_layout_hashes`, `macro` - never once includes it, confirmed by grep that
`file_sha256` is read nowhere else in the whole codebase either. Reproduced directly against a real
committed sample workbook (`templates/samples/R.334-030-2025.1F_ran.xlsm`), two ways: (1) a pure
metadata edit (`docProps/core.xml`'s creator field only) - every structural signal identical,
`file_sha256` differs; (2) a REAL content change (flipped one shared string's actual text, e.g. a
label like "TENDERER NAME:") - every structural signal STILL identical (`cell_layout_hashes` tracks
which cells are occupied, never what they say), `file_sha256` differs. Both cases: `diff()` returned
zero changes AND zero warnings - `main()`'s own CLI would print "OK: matches" with no trace either
case had happened at all.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, severe).** A genuine SANRAL-changed label, a re-worded instruction, or a
dropdown option's own text being silently edited between template revisions - exactly the category of
change Sarel's own standing rule exists to catch before a pack gets built against it - was completely
undetectable by this tool, directly contradicting the module's own stated job ("refuses to proceed
silently on any mismatch"). Blindly promoting `file_sha256` to a BLOCKING change was ruled out: the
metadata-only case above proves it would false-positive-block every trivial re-save (the exact "known-
noisy signal" shape this module's own docstring already documents for three OTHER fields), which would
likely cost Sarel's trust in the tool faster than the gap itself.

**Fix:** `file_sha256` now gets the SAME non-blocking-warning treatment the module already proved out
for `macro` - surfaced as its own warning (never blocking) whenever it differs AND no structural
change already explains why (redundant otherwise). Both real callers were then checked for whether
they'd actually SURFACE this new warning or silently drop it like they do today for `macro`:
`check_fingerprint()`'s own "OK" message hard-coded "macro-only difference, known to be benign" for
ANY non-empty warnings list - which would have silently mislabelled a real file_sha256 warning as
benign too, exactly undoing this fix's own point - fixed to branch on which warning actually fired.
`check_template()` computed `fingerprint.diff()`'s warnings (`soft`) and then never added them to its
own returned `warnings` list AT ALL - the real SANRAL pack-build path was silently dropping every
fingerprint warning, macro included, before this fix; now both flow through into `build_submission_
pack()`'s own warnings list, the one that reaches the pack's real manifest.

**Verified red-then-green.** `engine/test_fingerprint.py` (4 new checks: file_sha256-only difference
surfaces a warning and doesn't block, no warning when nothing differs, no redundant warning when a
real structural change already blocks); `engine/intake/test_classify_tender.py` (3 new checks: a
file_sha256-only difference says "have a person look at this template by eye", not "known to be
benign"; a macro-only difference is unaffected); `engine/pack/test_assemble_pack.py` (4 new checks:
both file_sha256 and macro warnings now reach `check_template()`'s own returned warnings, neither
blocks). Revert-and-confirm-red on all three files together: reverting reproduced exactly 1+1+2 = 4
predicted failures across the three test files, every other check (including every pre-existing
mismatch/corrupted-baseline/unfillable-family case) still green; restored, `0 failure(s)` across all
three. Also confirmed end to end via the real CLI (`python3 engine/fingerprint.py`) against the real
content-changed sample - the warning now prints exactly as designed. Regression-checked `engine/pack/
test_process_pack_jobs.py`, `engine/general/test_requirements.py` - all pass. `py_compile` clean on
all three touched production files.

**Regression:** `engine/fingerprint.py` (`diff()`: one new conditional block, ~5 lines - every
pre-existing comparison is byte-for-byte unaffected, confirmed by the full existing `test_fingerprint.
py` suite including the real named-ranges disambiguation fix staying green), `engine/intake/classify_
tender.py` (`check_fingerprint()`: the "ok" branch's message now branches on warning content instead
of a blanket "macro-only" assumption), `engine/pack/assemble_pack.py` (`check_template()`: `soft` is
now folded into the returned `warnings` list instead of discarded), plus the three corresponding test
files (11 new checks total across `test_fingerprint.py`/`test_classify_tender.py`/`test_assemble_
pack.py`). No schema or other call-site changes - both real callers' OWN return shapes are unchanged
(same dict keys / same `(family, warnings)` tuple), only what populates them.

### Finding 119 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a company's own uploaded CIDB registration/grading certificate could never reach a general (non-SANRAL) pack's "CIDB registration / grading" returnable, even when it was sitting right there in the vault - the same migration-0063 column a sibling pass independently found missing from watch_deadlines.py the same day)

**Where:** this cycle's non-SANRAL pack rotation. `engine/general/build_general_pack.py`'s
`VAULT_FILE_FOR`/`VAULT_EXPIRY_FOR`, and `engine/general/process_general_jobs.py`'s `VAULT_COLUMNS` -
the real, live general-pack-build path (`gather_pack_inputs()` downloads each vault file;
`build_general_pack()`'s own returnables loop, step 4, resolves one for each tender requirement).

**What was tested:** `requirements.RETURNABLES` carries a real `"cidb"` key ("CIDB registration /
grading") that every general pack's manifest can produce; `companies.cidb_document_path`/
`cidb_expiry` are real, live columns (migration `0063_onboarding_document_scan.sql`, confirmed
directly against the migration file and `app/lib/vaultDocuments.ts`'s own `VAULT_DOCUMENTS` catalog,
which already lists `cidb` as one of 7 vault document kinds). But `VAULT_FILE_FOR`/`VAULT_EXPIRY_FOR`
(5 entries each) and `VAULT_COLUMNS` (5 entries) never included it - confirmed by grep, zero mentions
of "cidb" anywhere in `build_general_pack.py`. Reproduced directly: a company dict carrying a real
`cidb_document_path` value, run through the exact lookup `build_general_pack()`'s own returnables
loop performs (`VAULT_FILE_FOR.get(r["key"])` after checking for a per-tender upload), resolved to
`None` - the vault document was never even looked for, let alone found.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Traced the full chain, not just the mapping dict: even fixing `VAULT_FILE_
FOR` alone would NOT have closed the gap - `process_general_jobs.py`'s own `VAULT_COLUMNS` (the list
controlling which vault columns actually get DOWNLOADED from Storage before the pack build starts)
was missing the same column, so the file would never even reach the local `files` dict for `VAULT_
FILE_FOR`'s lookup to find. A company that did everything right - uploaded a real CIDB certificate to
their vault - would see every general-tender pack claim "not uploaded for this tender" for that
returnable, with no mention a vault copy was even possible, forever (both gaps are structural, not
timing-dependent - this reproduces on every single affected pack build, not a rare race). Notably the
SAME migration-0063 column (`cidb_expiry`) was independently found missing from a DIFFERENT list
(`watch_deadlines.TRACKED_EXPIRY_FIELDS`) by a sibling QA pass earlier the same day - strong
convergent evidence that migration 0063 introduced real, live functionality that several pre-existing
lists across the codebase were never updated to include, a genuine "added a new column, forgot every
downstream consumer" shape rather than two unrelated coincidences.

**Fix:** added `"cidb": "cidb_document_path"` to `VAULT_FILE_FOR`, `"cidb": "cidb_expiry"` to `VAULT_
EXPIRY_FOR` (both in `build_general_pack.py`), and `"cidb_document_path"` to `process_general_jobs.
VAULT_COLUMNS` - the same 3-line-per-entry pattern every other vault document already uses. Swept the
rest of `engine/` for the same 5-item vault-column list shape (grep for the other four columns
together) to confirm no OTHER copy exists with the identical gap - `scenario_driver.py`'s own 3-column
subset is test/demo seeding, not a completeness-critical list, left as-is.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_cidb_vault_document_is_now_reachable_from_a_general_pack()`
to `engine/general/test_build_general_pack.py` (4 checks: `cidb` really is a real returnables key,
both dicts now map it to the real columns, `VAULT_COLUMNS` now downloads it, and the exact lookup
`build_general_pack()` itself runs now actually resolves to the vault file instead of `None`).
Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted 4 failures with every pre-existing
check in the file (the real misfiled-COID-incident case, the no-rule-for-pi_insurance/iso_9001/bank_
letter cases) still green; restored, `0 failure(s)`. Regression-checked `engine/general/test_process_
general_jobs.py`, `test_requirements.py` - all pass. `py_compile` clean on both touched production
files.

**Regression:** `engine/general/build_general_pack.py` (two dict entries added, ~12 lines including
comment), `engine/general/process_general_jobs.py` (one list entry added, ~5 lines including
comment), `engine/general/test_build_general_pack.py` (1 new test function, 4 checks, wired into
`main()`). No schema or other call-site changes - the columns already exist (migration `0063`, live
since it was applied); this fix only wires already-live data into an already-live code path.

### Finding 120 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a company's own confirmed SACPCMP registration date, already extracted and already stored, never once reached a generated CV document - two independent gaps, one in the display logic, one in the Supabase-backed bridge's own adapter)

**Where:** this cycle's CV rotation. `engine/cv/generate_cv.py`'s `build_sanral_keyperson()` (the
function that explicitly claims to mirror SANRAL's own real Form B2.1 exactly) and
`engine/cv/process_cv_jobs.py`'s `adapt_person_row()` (the adapter that turns a Supabase `people` row
into the profile dict `build_sanral_keyperson()` reads).

**What was tested:** `docs/specs/CV-Engine-Findings.md` (the evidence doc written before this engine
was built) states Form B2.1 shows "professional registration body + level + number + date
(ECSA/SACPCMP)" - date, for BOTH bodies, not just ECSA. Confirmed against the real, live SANRAL-form
filler: `engine/fill_tender.py`'s and `engine/fill_conventional.py`'s own cell-offset dict both carry
`sacpcmp_date="P41"` as a real, distinct cell on the actual completed workbook, and `fill_person()`
writes `q.get("sacpcmp_date")` into it whenever present - proving the real form genuinely has this
field, it isn't a misreading of the spec. `people.sacpcmp_date` (migration `0001_init_schema.sql`,
same table/migration as `sacpcmp_number`) is a real, live column: `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py`'s
own `PERSON_DATE_FIELDS` already extracts it from an uploaded CV via AI, and a completely separate
pipeline, `engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py`'s `adapt_person()` (line ~273), already reads it
correctly into the SANRAL pack-build path. But `generate_cv.py`'s `build_sanral_keyperson()` - the one
function whose entire job is producing a portable Word/PDF CV that mirrors this exact form - only ever
printed `q.get("sacpcmp_number")`, never `q.get("sacpcmp_date")`, even though the row directly above it
in the same table shows ECSA's level, number, AND date, all three. Confirmed by grep: `sacpcmp_date` is
read nowhere in `generate_cv.py` before this fix.

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Traced the full chain rather than stopping at the display gap, the same
discipline Finding 119 used: even if `build_sanral_keyperson()` alone were fixed, the real,
Supabase-backed CV-generation path (`process_cv_jobs.py`'s `process_job()` -> `fetch_job_context()` ->
`adapt_person_row()`) would still never surface the date, because `adapt_person_row()`'s own
qualifications dict carried `sacpcmp_number` through but never read `person_row.get("sacpcmp_date")`
at all - confirmed by grep, and by direct inspection of the dict literal. A company whose key person
has a real, AI-extracted SACPCMP registration date on file (the same date `extract_cv_fields.py`
already captured and the SANRAL pack builder already uses) would see it correctly appear in a merged
SANRAL submission pack, but the standalone CV document generated for that same person - whether via
the CLI/JSON path (display gap only) or the live Supabase-backed "Generate tender-specific CV" button
(both gaps stacked) - silently omitted it, every single time, not a rare race.

**Fix:** added a `"SACPCMP registration date:"` row to `build_sanral_keyperson()`'s own `rows` list in
`engine/cv/generate_cv.py`, immediately after the existing `"SACPCMP number:"` row, reading
`q.get("sacpcmp_date") or "MISSING"` - the same unconditional-row, honest-"MISSING"-fallback pattern
already used for ECSA's own date field two rows above it; the file's existing per-row provenance
classification loop (`if value in ("MISSING", "Not registered / not on file"): log.missing(...)`)
needed no change, since it already treats "MISSING" correctly. Added `"sacpcmp_date":
person_row.get("sacpcmp_date")` to `process_cv_jobs.py`'s `adapt_person_row()` qualifications dict, the
same one-line-per-field pattern every other field in that dict already uses.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_sacpcmp_registration_date_now_appears_on_form_b21()` and
`test_sacpcmp_registration_date_missing_degrades_honestly()` to `engine/cv/test_generate_cv.py` (3
checks: the date is printed on the real document when present, logged as confirmed with the right
value; logged as missing with a reason when absent, not silently blank). Added
`test_adapt_person_row_carries_sacpcmp_date_through()` to `engine/cv/test_process_cv_jobs.py` (2

### Finding 122 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a re-assessed/downgraded tender's "Re-assessed tenders" digest line never showed WHY it was no longer a good fit, only the tender's own generic title - the exact same bug class Finding 113 fixed for listing_changes, left unfixed for a second, independent section)

**Where:** this cycle's notify rotation. `engine/notify/send_digest_emails.py`'s `render_text()`.

**What was tested:** read `render_text()`'s own `bit`-selection chain end to end, alongside every
place in `engine/` that sets a `"summary"` key on a digest item (grepped: exactly two,
`discovery/tender_changes.py` for `listing_changes` items, and `discovery/discovery_downgrades.py`'s
`pending_digest_downgrades()` for `reassessed_tenders` items). Finding 113 (2026-11-01) fixed
`listing_changes`' own "title wins unconditionally, summary never shown" bug by appending `summary`
whenever `item.get("change_type") and item.get("summary")` - deliberately scoped to `"change_type"`
as a safe, unique discriminator (confirmed by that fix's own comment: "no other section sets it").
But `discovery_downgrades.py`'s `reassessed_tenders` items carry the identical shape of fact in their
own `"summary"` (e.g. `"No longer a good fit: was strong_fit, now possible..."`) without ever setting
`"change_type"` at all (confirmed by grep: `was_verdict`/`now_verdict` are its own unique keys
instead) - so Finding 113's own fix, scoped only to `change_type`, silently never applied to this
section, which didn't exist as a digest section yet at the time that fix's "no other section sets it"
grep was done (or simply wasn't re-checked against it).

**Finding (CONFIRMED).** Every reassessed-tender line in a sent digest showed only the tender's own
generic title - already shown in every other section of the same email - with the one fact this whole
section exists to report (a tender a company was tracking is no longer a good fit, and why) never
reaching the actual sent email text. A company relying on the digest to flag tenders worth dropping
would see "Routine maintenance of provincial roads" and nothing else - no indication it had been
downgraded, from what, to what, or why.

**Fix:** widened the condition to `(item.get("change_type") or item.get("was_verdict")) and
item.get("summary"):` - `was_verdict` confirmed unique to `reassessed_tenders` items by grep, the same
discipline Finding 113 used for `change_type`. Deliberately NOT widened to a bare `item.get("summary")`:
`tender_updates` items (`watch_tender_updates.pending_digest_updates()`) also carry a `"summary"` key
with a different meaning (a watched document's own AI-generated summary) that Finding 113's own test
already locks in as deliberately unshown via this path - a bare `summary` check would have silently
started showing that unrelated text too.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_render_text_shows_why_a_tender_was_reassessed()` to
`test_send_digest_emails.py` (2 checks: the reassessed-tender line now shows both the tender title and
the real reason; the existing `tender_updates` regression guard from Finding 113's own test still
holds after the widening). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced exactly the 1 predicted
failure, every pre-existing check (including Finding 113's own listing_changes/tender_updates checks)
staying green; restored, `0 failure(s)`. Regression-checked `test_digest_live.py` and
`test_digest_opt_in.py` - both clean. `py_compile` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/notify/send_digest_emails.py` (one condition widened, ~14 lines including
comment), `engine/notify/test_send_digest_emails.py` (1 new test function, 2 checks, wired into
`main()`). No schema or call-site changes - `discovery_downgrades.py`'s own `pending_digest_downgrades()`
already computed `summary` correctly; this fix only lets the existing email renderer show it.

### Finding 123 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, severe - a bridge subprocess failing to even START (not just timing out or exiting non-zero) silently aborted the WHOLE worker cycle and reached no alert at all in --loop mode, the one mode the real container actually runs)

**Where:** this cycle's worker/job-queue rotation. `engine/worker/run_bridges.py`'s
`BridgeRunner.run_once()`.

**What was tested:** `run_once()`'s own loop already guards two bridge-pass failure shapes carefully
(a hung bridge, killed by its whole process group per the 2026-10-23 fix; a bridge that exits
non-zero) - both `broken.append(...)` and alert via `system_alerts.record(label, ...)`, then continue
to the next bridge. But `subprocess.Popen(...)` itself (launching the subprocess, not waiting on it)
sat OUTSIDE both of those try blocks, unguarded. Reproduced directly: monkeypatched `subprocess.Popen`
to raise `OSError("Cannot allocate memory")` on the first call (simulating a real, reachable fork
failure under memory pressure - plausible for this exact container, which this file's own docstring
says may be mid-soffice/LibreOffice work for a pack bridge when a second bridge's turn comes up in the
same cycle) and ran `BridgeRunner.run_once()` against two registered bridges.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, severe).** The raw `OSError` propagated straight out of `run_once()`, uncaught:
(1) the loop aborted entirely - the SECOND bridge was never even attempted that cycle, not just the
failing one (confirmed: only 1 `Popen()` call recorded before the test's own exception assertions);
(2) zero calls reached `system_alerts.record()` - the failure never got the per-bridge alert treatment
every other failure shape in this same function already gets. In `--once` mode this exception does
still reach the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard's own fallback (`except Exception: system_alerts.
record("worker", ...)`) - no real gap there. But in `--loop` mode - explicitly the ONLY mode the real
worker container runs, per this file's own docstring ("what the container runs") - `runner.run_once`
is called as `poll_loop.poll_forever()`'s own `poll_once` callback, which wraps it in a GENERIC
per-cycle `except Exception` that only `print()`s and counts an error, never calling `system_alerts.
record()` at all unless an `alert_source` was passed to `poll_forever()` - and `run_bridges.py`'s own
call in `main()` never passes one. So in production, a `Popen()`-level failure (fork failure, a broken
interpreter path, a permissions issue) was silently lost: not in system_alerts, only in a container log
nobody watches (the entire reason `system_alerts` exists per this codebase's own standing practice).

**Fix:** wrapped the `Popen(...)` call itself in `try/except OSError`, treating a failure to even
start a bridge the same way as every other failure shape in this function: `broken.append(...)` +
`system_alerts.record(label, ..., "critical", ...)` under that bridge's OWN source, then `continue` to
the next bridge rather than aborting the whole cycle. Deliberately did NOT add a blanket `alert_source`
to the `poll_forever()` call in `main()` as a second line of defense: `poll_forever`'s own generic
catch fires on the ordinary `RuntimeError` `run_once()` already raises for every per-bridge failure
too, which already gets its own, more specific alert recorded inside `run_once()` - adding
`alert_source` there would double-alert on the common, already-well-handled path (timeout/non-zero
exit) to guard a now-much-narrower residual gap, not a clean improvement.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added `test_a_bridge_that_fails_to_even_start_is_reported_not_silently_lost()`
to `engine/worker/test_poll_loop.py`, in the same real-subprocess, no-mock-framework style as this
file's existing `test_timeout_kills_the_whole_process_group()`: monkeypatches `subprocess.Popen` to
fail only on the first call, confirms the SECOND bridge still runs (loop doesn't abort), confirms
exactly one `system_alerts.record()` call under the failing bridge's own label with `"critical"`
severity. Ran the full `test_poll_loop.py` suite (every real end-to-end bridge-loop smoke test, not
just the new one) - all pass. Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted raw
`OSError` escaping uncaught; restored, all tests pass again. `py_compile`/`ast.parse` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/worker/run_bridges.py` (one `try/except` added around the `Popen()` call,
~20 lines including comment), `engine/worker/test_poll_loop.py` (1 new test function, wired into the
file's own `__main__` runner). No change to the timeout/non-zero-exit handling already in place, and
no change to `--once` mode's own existing correct behavior.

### Finding 124 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, severe - one malformed row anywhere in SANRAL's own AJAX tender-list response crashed list_tenders.py's whole parse, losing every OTHER real, open tender in that response too, not just the bad row)

**Where:** this cycle's discovery rotation. `engine/discovery/list_tenders.py`'s `fetch_tenders()`/
`_parse_row()` - the reader SANRAL's own open/awarded/closed lists go through (`gov_sources.
sanral_releases()`, the primary production call path via `watch_new_tenders.py`, and
`award_outcomes.py`'s own paged reader).

**What was tested:** `_parse_row(row)` unpacks exactly `ref_cell, project_type, province,
description, queries_to, closing_date = row[:6]` - no test file existed for this module at all
before this pass. The module's own docstring already documents SANRAL's response as observably
inconsistent ("total_filtered" (observed 139) not always equal to the actual row count returned
(observed 137) - "this script does not try to explain that discrepancy"), so a single short/malformed
row among ~137 good ones is a realistic, not theoretical, shape for this government site to produce.
Constructed a real adversarial payload: two genuine, well-formed 6-cell tender rows plus one
malformed 3-cell row in between, fed through a faked `urllib.request.urlopen` (no real network
call), and ran `fetch_tenders()` against it.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, severe).** `row[:6]` on a 3-cell row is just a 3-element slice - the 6-way
unpack then raises `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 6, got 3)`, straight out of
`fetch_tenders()`'s own list comprehension (`[_parse_row(r) for r in payload.get("tenders", [])]`).
Confirmed directly: with the fix reverted, the SAME adversarial payload returned ZERO tenders and
raised, rather than the two real, well-formed ones. `gov_sources.fetch_all()`'s own per-source
try/except does catch this one level up and alert "SANRAL source failed" (via
`watch_new_tenders.py`'s own system_alerts call) rather than crashing the whole multi-source
discovery run - so the failure isn't silent - but the actual cost is still severe: the ENTIRE
SANRAL source (SANRAL being the primary, highest-volume real tender source this project tracks, not
a minor one) returns nothing for that day's run over a single bad row, discarding every other
genuinely open tender in the same response along with it.

**Fix:** added a length check to `_parse_row()` (`if len(row) < 6: raise ValueError(...)` with the
real cell count in the message, replacing Python's own generic "not enough values to unpack"), and -
the real fix - wrapped each row's `_parse_row(r)` call in `fetch_tenders()`'s own loop in a per-row
`try/except (ValueError, TypeError)`, skipping and logging a warning for the one bad row while still
returning every other real tender in the response. Added a `log=print` parameter to `fetch_tenders()`
(every sibling scraper in this codebase - `kouga.py`, `dbsa_procurement.py`, etc. - already takes one
for exactly this purpose; `list_tenders.py` was the one without it, so it had no way to surface a
per-row warning to its real caller at all) and threaded it through both real call sites:
`gov_sources.sanral_releases()` (which already receives its own `log` parameter, just never passed it
on) and `list_tenders.main()` (now logs to stderr, matching this file's own existing stderr
convention).

**Verified red-then-green.** New file `engine/discovery/test_list_tenders.py` (3 tests: a real
well-formed row parses correctly; a short row raises a clear, actionable `ValueError` naming the real
cell count; a response with one bad row among two good ones returns both good tenders with exactly
one warning logged, not a crash). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted
breakage (the unpack-crash message instead of the clearer one; `fetch_tenders()` raising `TypeError`
for the now-unsupported `log=` kwarg, confirming the whole fix chain); restored, `0 failure(s)`.
Regression-checked `test_gov_sources.py` and `test_award_outcomes.py` (both already real end-to-end
test suites covering this file's own callers) - all pass, unaffected. `py_compile`/`ast.parse` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/discovery/list_tenders.py` (a length check plus a per-row try/except in
`fetch_tenders()`, a new `log` parameter, ~20 lines including comments), `engine/discovery/gov_sources.py`
(one call site now threads its own existing `log` parameter through, 1 line),
`engine/discovery/test_list_tenders.py` (new file, 3 tests). No change to the response shape any
caller reads - `rows`/`total`/`total_filtered` are returned exactly as before, just now with bad rows
skipped instead of the whole batch lost.

### Finding 125 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, severe - a single control character anywhere in a tender's OCR'd description or delivery address crashed ALL THREE envelope cover sheets, taking down the WHOLE SANRAL pack build - not a cosmetic miss, since assemble_pack.py's own envelope-covers step has no try/except around it)

**Where:** this cycle's SANRAL pack rotation. `engine/make_envelope_covers.py` - no dedicated test
file or QA pass found anywhere in this file's history, despite being a real production call site
(`assemble_pack.py`'s own envelope-covers step, step 6 of `build_submission_pack()`).

**What was tested:** read the file end to end. Every text field it prints into a cover (`contract_no`,
`nra_ref`, `description`, `delivery_address` lines, the company's own `legal_name`/
`registered_address`/`cipc_registration_number`) is read from a real, uncontrolled source -
`description`/`nra_ref`/`delivery_address` straight out of a tender's own scanned/OCR'd document text
(`classify_tender.find_nra_reference()`/`find_delivery_address()`, confirmed by reading those
functions' own call chain back to `requirements.py`'s OCR path). This codebase has already found and
fixed the identical bug class once before, in a different file: `generate_cv.py`'s own `_safe_text()`
exists specifically because python-docx (via lxml) raises `ValueError("All strings must be XML
compatible...")` on a control character, confirmed there as a realistic OCR artifact. `make_envelope_
covers.py` had no equivalent sanitizer at all - confirmed directly: `python3 -c "import docx; docx.
Document().add_paragraph('Routine ad-hoc\x0bmaintenance...')"` raises that exact `ValueError`.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, severe).** `_addressee_block()`/`_tender_block()`/`_bidder_block()` all call
`d.add_paragraph(...)` directly on these externally-sourced strings with no sanitization. Traced the
real caller rather than stopping at "python-docx can raise here": `assemble_pack.py`'s own
envelope-covers step (building `covers = {"outer": make_envelope_covers.make_outer(...), "technical":
..., "financial": ...}`) has **no try/except around it at all** - unlike the file's own financial/C2.4
print step just above it, which already degrades gracefully with a warning on failure. A single
control character anywhere in a tender's description or delivery address (both read from OCR'd
document text, the exact source this codebase already knows is capable of misreading characters)
would crash `make_outer()` on its very first paragraph, propagating straight out of
`build_submission_pack()` and failing the ENTIRE pack job - every form, every returnable, the merged
PDF - not just the three cover sheets, which are a minor, cosmetic part of a SANRAL submission pack
next to the technical/financial workbook and returnables.

**Fix:** added the identical `_XML_INVALID_RE`/`_safe_text()` pattern `generate_cv.py` already uses
(same regex, same approach - strip control characters rather than crash or silently truncate), applied
to every `add_paragraph()` call on an externally-sourced string: `contract_no`/`nra_ref`/`description`
(folded into one interpolated string in `_tender_block()`), every `delivery_address` line, the
`closing_date`/`closing_time` line, and the company's `legal_name`/`registered_address`/
`cipc_registration_number`. Did not touch the two fixed, hardcoded pricing-statement strings or the
envelope heading text - those are never externally sourced.

**Verified red-then-green.** New file `engine/test_make_envelope_covers.py` (4 tests, no network, no
real docx template needed: a control character in `description` doesn't crash `make_outer()`; one in a
`delivery_address` line doesn't crash `make_inner()`; one in each of the three company fields doesn't
crash `make_outer()` and is stripped from the real output while the surrounding real text survives
intact; ordinary clean text is returned byte-identical, no over-stripping). Revert-and-confirm-red:
reverting reproduced the exact predicted `ValueError` on all three crash tests plus an `AttributeError`
for the now-missing `_safe_text` on the fourth; restored, `0 failure(s)`. Regression-checked
`engine/pack/test_assemble_pack.py` (this file's own real caller's test suite) - all pass, unaffected.
`py_compile` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/make_envelope_covers.py` (one new regex + helper, ~22 lines including comment;
6 call sites wrapped), `engine/test_make_envelope_covers.py` (new file, 4 tests). No change to any
cover's visible text for the overwhelmingly common case (no control characters) - confirmed by the new
no-op regression test.

### Finding 126 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a transient claim failure on one CV upload aborted the whole extraction cycle, silently skipping every OTHER genuinely pending upload in the same batch, not just the one whose claim failed)

**Where:** this cycle's CV rotation. `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py`'s `poll_once()`.

**What was tested:** `process_upload()` already has thorough per-exception handling (`SetupError`/
`TransientError`/`ExtractionFailed`/generic `Exception`, each with its own recovery path) - but all of
it lives INSIDE a `try:` block that starts AFTER `claim_upload(url, key, upload)` is called. Reproduced
directly: monkeypatched `claim_upload`'s own `supabase_request()` call to raise `RuntimeError`
(simulating a transient Supabase blip - a real, realistic failure mode, the same shape `run_bridges.py`'s
own Finding 123 guarded against for a bridge's subprocess launch) for the first of two queued uploads,
and ran `poll_once()` against both.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, moderate).** The `RuntimeError` propagated straight out of `process_upload()`,
uncaught by any of its own exception handlers (all scoped to after the claim), and then straight out of
`poll_once()`'s own `for up in uploads:` loop - which had NO per-item isolation at all. Confirmed: only
the first upload was even attempted; the second, genuinely pending, otherwise-fine upload was never
even reached that cycle. Same "one bad item must not cost everyone else in the same pass" bug class
this codebase has already found and fixed repeatedly (`daily_digest.py`'s own per-roster-entry
isolation, explicitly citing "one bad roster entry must not cost everyone else their digest";
`run_bridges.py`'s own per-bridge isolation, Finding 123, the previous cycle). In `--loop` mode this
particular instance is at least correctly alerted (unlike Finding 123's `run_bridges.py` gap -
`extract_cv_fields.py`'s own `run()` already passes `alert_source="cv_extract"` to `poll_forever()`),
so it isn't silent, but it still means every other pending company's CV extraction request waits an
extra cycle (or indefinitely, if the same upload keeps sorting first and keeps failing) for no reason
tied to their own request at all.

**Fix:** wrapped the `process_upload(...)` call inside `poll_once()`'s own loop in a `try/except`,
alerting under `"cv_extract"` and continuing to the next upload - mirroring the exact pattern
`daily_digest.py`/`run_bridges.py` already use. Deliberately re-raises `SetupError` specifically rather
than swallowing it: a `SetupError` (missing API key, package not installed) means the WHOLE bridge is
broken, not one bad item, and `process_upload()` already re-raises it on purpose for exactly that
reason (its own comment: "recorded by whoever runs the pass") - catching it here too would have masked
that distinction, having every subsequent upload in the batch independently retry and alert on the
same already-known-broken setup instead of stopping the pass cleanly. `TransientError`/
`ExtractionFailed` were already fully handled inside `process_upload()` itself (never re-raised), so
this new catch only ever reaches the specific gap this finding guards: `claim_upload()`'s own call
site and any other code outside `process_upload()`'s own try block.

**Verified red-then-green.** Added a new scenario to `test_queue()` in `test_extract_cv_fields.py`
(using the file's existing `MemoryDb`/`flaky_request`-monkeypatching convention): one upload (`u7`)
whose claim raises, one (`u8`) that should still succeed in the same cycle. 3 checks: `u7` is left
`extraction_requested` (not stuck half-claimed); `u8` is still processed (the bug this test guards);
`u7`'s own failure is still reported as its own alert, not silently lost. Also verified separately
that `SetupError` still propagates correctly out of `poll_once()` (the whole-bridge-broken case must
not be swallowed). Revert-and-confirm-red: reverting reproduced the exact predicted uncaught
`RuntimeError`, with the traceback landing precisely at `claim_upload()`'s own call site; restored, ALL
PASSED (every pre-existing check in this file's large test suite, unaffected). `py_compile`/
`ast.parse` clean.

**Regression:** `engine/cv/extract_cv_fields.py` (one `try/except` added around the per-upload loop
body in `poll_once()`, ~15 lines including comment), `engine/cv/test_extract_cv_fields.py` (1 new
scenario inside the existing `test_queue()` function, 3 checks). No change to any already-handled
failure path (`SetupError`/`TransientError`/`ExtractionFailed` all behave exactly as before).

### Finding 127 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - a CANCELLED notification workflow run never recorded a heartbeat "finish" at all, in all 10 of the notification-sending GitHub Actions workflows, leaving it stuck showing "running" until a generic staleness timeout, instead of correctly and immediately reported as cancelled)

**Where:** this cycle's notify rotation. All 10 notification-sending GitHub Actions workflows
(`.github/workflows/{compliance-alerts,corrigendum-alerts,daily-digest,daily-discovery,
deadline-reminders,founder-digest,onboarding-nudges,operational-alerts,returnables-digest,
scout-alerts}.yml`) and `engine/notify/record_heartbeat.py`'s own module docstring.

**What was tested:** `record_heartbeat.py`'s own docstring claims it is "wired as the FIRST and LAST
steps of each of the 9 notification-sending workflows." Counted directly (`grep -l "record_heartbeat.py
start" .github/workflows/*.yml`): 10, not 9 - a separate, minor, pre-existing drift, not something
this pass introduced. Read each of the 10 real workflows' own heartbeat wiring end to end: each has a
"Record heartbeat (start)" step first, then two separate "finish" steps at the end - one
`if: success()`, one `if: failure()` - with each file's own comment explicitly explaining WHY two
steps instead of one `if: always()` ("GitHub Actions has no single 'did the job pass' value available
mid-job, only the success()/failure() context functions on separate steps"). This same codebase
already independently discovered and documented, in a DIFFERENT workflow (`bridge-worker-ci.yml`,
2026-10-19), that GitHub Actions' own `cancelled()` context function is a THIRD, SEPARATE state from
`success()`/`failure()` - but that lesson was never carried over to these 10 heartbeat `if: failure()`
conditions.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, moderate).** Per GitHub Actions' own documented semantics (confirmed consistent
with this repo's own prior, independent discovery of the exact same distinction in
`bridge-worker-ci.yml`): `success()` is true only when nothing before it failed or was cancelled;
`failure()` is true only when something before it genuinely failed; NEITHER is true when the run was
CANCELLED (a concurrency-group supersede, a manual cancel from the Actions UI, GitHub's own
workflow-level timeout). So a cancelled run of any of these 10 workflows never ran either "finish"
step at all - its heartbeat's own "start" row was left showing "running" forever, with no finish call
ever recording what actually happened. Each workflow's own comment already notes the admin UI has a
staleness check that eventually flags a stuck "running" row - so this isn't a silently-lost-forever
failure, but it means a cancelled run is reported late and as a generic "stuck," not immediately and
correctly as "cancelled," even though GitHub itself already knows precisely what happened at the
moment it happens.

**Fix:** changed the "Record heartbeat (failure)" step's condition from `if: failure()` to `if:
failure() || cancelled()` in all 10 workflows, and updated each file's own comment to explain the
cancelled() gap explicitly (mirroring the reasoning already proven correct in `bridge-worker-ci.yml`).
Also reworded each failure step's own `--error` message from "One or more steps in this job failed"
to "One or more steps in this job failed or the run was cancelled" so the recorded reason stays
accurate for both causes under the one `"failed"` status value (no new status value needed -
`record_heartbeat.py`'s own `finish()` already only accepts `success`/`failed`). Separately corrected
`record_heartbeat.py`'s own docstring from "9" to "10" notification-sending workflows.

**Verified.** These are GitHub Actions YAML workflow files, not Python under unit test - verified by
(1) parsing all 10 with `yaml.safe_load()` after editing (all valid), (2) confirming the new
`if: failure() || cancelled()` syntax matches GitHub Actions' own documented, standard expression
grammar and this repo's own already-proven `cancelled()` usage pattern in `bridge-worker-ci.yml`
exactly, (3) re-running `engine/notify/test_record_heartbeat.py` after the docstring edit to
`record_heartbeat.py` itself - `9 passed, 0 failed`, unaffected (the Python logic itself didn't
change, only the YAML callers' own trigger conditions). `py_compile` clean on the Python file.

**Regression:** 10 workflow YAML files (one condition changed, one comment expanded, and one error
message reworded per file - no change to any already-correct `success()` path or to the business-logic
steps themselves), `engine/notify/record_heartbeat.py` (docstring count correction only, no logic
change). No change to `record_heartbeat.py`'s own `finish()` function or its accepted `status` values.

### Finding 128 (CONFIRMED, FIXED, moderate - the deliberate sweep: the "claim call sits outside its own try block, with no per-item isolation in the polling loop" bug class, found and fixed once in run_bridges.py (Finding 123) and once in extract_cv_fields.py (Finding 126), was present in all FOUR remaining job-queue bridges too)

**Where:** this cycle's worker/job-queue rotation. `engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py`'s `process_pending()`,

**What was tested:** explicitly flagged in Finding 126's own write-up as worth a deliberate sweep
rather than finding a fourth instance one file at a time - checked all four remaining bridges for the
identical shape: a `claim_job()`/`claim_upload()`/`client.update(...)` claim call sitting BEFORE its
own function's `try:` block, with the per-job/per-upload polling loop having no isolation of its own
around that call.

**Finding (CONFIRMED, moderate - found in all four).** Every one of the four had the exact same shape:
`process_job()`/`process_one()`/`process_upload()` already has thorough exception handling for
everything AFTER the claim (each one's own blanket `except Exception`, or - in
`process_narrative_jobs.py`/`process_onboarding_jobs.py`, which call an LLM - a deliberately re-raised

jobs:`/`for up in uploads:`) has zero per-item isolation. Reproduced directly for each: a simulated
transient claim failure (a network blip, a 500) on the FIRST of two queued items propagated straight
out of the loop, aborting the whole pass - confirmed the SECOND, genuinely pending item was never even
attempted in all four cases. Also found a related, independent gap specific to
`process_narrative_jobs.py`: its own standalone `--loop` mode's `poll_forever()` call never passed
`name`/`alert_source` at all (every sibling bridge - `cv_extract`/`pack`/`general`/`onboarding` -
already does), so an exception that genuinely escapes this bridge's own new per-item isolation (a
`SetupError`) would have been swallowed by `poll_forever()`'s own generic catch with only a `print()`
in that mode - the same class of gap Finding 123 fixed for `run_bridges.py`.

**Fix:** wrapped the per-item call in each of the four polling loops in its own `try/except`, alerting
under that bridge's own existing `system_alerts` source (`"pack"`/`"general"`/`"narrative"`/
`"onboarding_scan"`) and continuing to the next item - identical pattern to Findings 123/126.
`process_narrative_jobs.py` and `process_onboarding_jobs.py` deliberately re-raise `SetupError`/
`cd.SetupError` specifically (the whole-bridge-broken case each file's own `process_one()`/
`process_upload()` already re-raises on purpose), not swallowing it. Also added the missing
`name="process_narrative_jobs", alert_source="narrative"` to that file's own standalone `--loop` mode
`poll_forever()` call.

**Verified red-then-green, all four, independently.** Added one new test per bridge (`test_process_pack_jobs.py`,
`test_process_general_jobs.py`, `test_process_narrative_jobs.py`, `test_process_onboarding_jobs.py`),
each monkeypatching the bridge's own `process_job`/`process_one`/`process_upload` to fail for one item
and succeed for a second, confirming BOTH items are attempted and the failing one gets its own alert.
`process_narrative_jobs.py`/`process_onboarding_jobs.py` each got a second test confirming `SetupError`/
`cd.SetupError` still correctly propagates out of `poll_once()` rather than being swallowed by the new
isolation. Revert-and-confirm-red on each of the four production files individually: each reproduced
the exact predicted uncaught exception at precisely the claim call site; restored, `0 failure(s)` on
all four, plus every pre-existing check in each file's test suite unaffected. Full regression sweep
across every bridge touched this session (`run_bridges.py`/`test_poll_loop.py`,
`extract_cv_fields.py`/`test_extract_cv_fields.py`, and all four fixed here) - all clean.
`py_compile` clean on all eight touched files.

**Regression:** `engine/pack/process_pack_jobs.py`, `engine/general/process_general_jobs.py`,
`engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py` (plus its missing `alert_source`),
`engine/onboarding/process_onboarding_jobs.py` (one `try/except` added per file's own polling loop, ~15
lines including comment each); `engine/pack/test_process_pack_jobs.py`,
`engine/general/test_process_general_jobs.py`, `engine/narrative/test_process_narrative_jobs.py`,
